children.text: Thank y'all so much for participating!
Farmer John can choose to build on every field that Farmer Nhoj does not own. Therefore, the answer is the number of farms in which Farmer Nhoj owns all the fields.
A bit on the harder side

When comparing two numbers that are initially not equal, the only way they can become equal after some number of operations is if at least one of them has an operation performed on it when it is $$$ \lt 2$$$.
If two elements are equal at some point, they'll be equal no matter how many more operations are performed. Therefore, it suffices to look at the end behavior of each element.
If $$$a_i\bmod 2 = 1$$$, then repeating the operation will eventually result in $$$a_i$$$ being equal to $$$1$$$.

If $$$a_i\bmod 4 = 0$$$, then repeating the operation will eventually result in $$$a_i$$$ being equal to $$$0$$$ when the number of operations performed is even and $$$a_i$$$ being equal to $$$2$$$ when the number of operations performed is odd.

If $$$a_i\bmod 4 = 2$$$, then repeating the operation will eventually result in $$$a_i$$$ being equal to $$$2$$$ when the number of operations performed is even and $$$a_i$$$ being equal to $$$0$$$ when the number of operations performed is odd.
Therefore, we can make two numbers equal to each other if they are both odd or both equal$$$\bmod 4$$$.

Since odd numbers will always equal $$$1$$$ or $$$3$$$ $$$(\bmod 4)$$$, we can not make any number that was originally odd equal to any number that was originally even. And since any even number initially divisible by $$$4$$$ will only be divisible by $$$4$$$ after an even number of operations, and any number $$$\equiv 2 \pmod 4$$$ will only be divisible by $$$4$$$ after an odd number of operations, we can't make two even numbers with different values $$$\bmod 4$$$ equal to eachother. Therefore, our answer is $$$\max(\text{# odd numbers}, \text{# numbers}\mod 4 = 0, \text{# numbers}\mod 4 = 2)$$$.
A bit on the harder side
If a $$$-1$$$ is in between two $$$1$$$s, it would only hurt the answer to make it a $$$1$$$.
If a $$$-1$$$ is not in between two $$$1$$$ s, the $$$-1$$$ would only be included in a subarray satisfying the conditions if it was an endpoint.

Consider the first $$$-1$$$ in $$$a$$$ at index $$$i$$$. If there is no $$$1$$$ before index $$$i$$$, then the $$$i$$$-th element can't be included in a subarray unless it is set to $$$1$$$. We can apply similar logic to the last $$$-1$$$ in $$$a$$$.

Now if there are no $$$1$$$s in $$$a$$$ once we perform the above, the answer is $$$0$$$. If there is one $$$1$$$ in $$$a$$$, the answer is $$$1$$$. The rest of the editorial assumes that there are at least $$$2$$$ $$$1$$$s in $$$a$$$.

Now every remaining $$$-1$$$ in $$$a$$$ is enclosed between two $$$1$$$s. If we set every $$$-1$$$ in between the $$$1$$$s to $$$0$$$, we can select that entire subarray. However, if we set at least one of those $$$-1$$$s to $$$1$$$, then we can no longer select the same subarray and would either have to select a subarray that does not involve that "region" or a shorter subarray.

Therefore, the optimal strategy is to set the first $$$-1$$$ to $$$1$$$ if there is no $$$1$$$ before it, the last $$$-1$$$ to $$$1$$$ if there is no $$$1$$$ after it, and the rest of the $$$-1$$$s to $$$0$$$.
A bit on the harder side
If there is only one $$$0$$$ in the array, then exactly one set will have a mex greater than zero
If there are no $$$0$$$s in $$$a$$$, any partitioning would result in each set having a MEX of $$$0$$$, trivially satisfying the condition.
If there is one $$$0$$$ in $$$a$$$, any partitioning would result in exactly $$$1$$$ set having a MEX greater than $$$0$$$, which would violate the condition.

If there are at least two $$$0$$$s in $$$a$$$, put the first $$$0$$$ in $$$A$$$, any other zeroes in $$$B$$$, and all non-zero elements in $$$C$$$. This makes $$$MEX(A) = MEX(B) = 1, MEX(C) = 0$$$, so $$$MEX(A) + MEX(B) + MEX(C) = 2 \geq 2 \cdot \max(MEX(A), MEX(B), MEX(C)) = 2$$$.
A bit on the harder side
If an element $$$x$$$ at index $$$i$$$ is not equal to $$$-1$$$, there must be a treasure at either island $$$i + x$$$ or $$$i - x$$$
If an element $$$x$$$ at index $$$i$$$ is not equal to $$$-1$$$, there must no treasures in the exclusive range of indices ($$$i + x$$$, $$$i - x$$$)
Let's consider all elements of $$$b$$$ that have not been destroyed. For the element $$$x$$$ at index $$$i$$$ to be valid, two conditions must be satisfied:
There must be no treasure in the range $$$max(1, i-x+1)\ldots min(n, i+x-1)$$$.
There must be a treasure at index $$$i - x$$$ and / or at index $$$i + x$$$.

For the first condition, the ranges that a treasure is forbidden to be at can be maintained using a difference array or any other technique that allows you to find all indexes covered by at least one range.
For the second condition, we can place a treasure on all non-forbidden indexes. Then, we can check if our construction works, and if so, output it.
A bit on the harder side
Look at performing some bubbles and reverse bubbles on small arrays. How many elements are moved?
A bubble will result is the leftmost 1 being moved all the way to the right. Similarly, a reverse bubble will result in the rightmost 0 being moved all the way to the left.

Since prefix zeroes and suffix ones don't matter, if we continuously remove them, then a bubble removes the last element of the array and a reverse bubble removes the first element of the array. Is there a way to remove the first and last elements of an array in constant time?

A bubble is equivalent to moving the first $$$1$$$ in $$$a$$$ to the end of $$$a$$$. To show this, look at each maximal subsegment of ones in $$$a$$$, which we will refer to as a run of ones. When we perform a bubble, we take the last $$$1$$$ in the first run of ones and repeatedly perform swaps to move that $$$1$$$ to the beginning of the second run of $$$1$$$s. Then, we perform swaps to move the last $$$1$$$ in the second run of ones to the beginning of the third run of ones, and so on until we either move a $$$1$$$ to the beginning of the last run of ones in $$$a$$$ (if the last element of $$$a$$$ is $$$1$$$) or to the end of $$$a$$$ (if the last element of $$$a$$$ is $$$0$$$).
Using the reverse logic, we can see that a reverse bubble is equivalent to moving the last $$$0$$$ in $$$a$$$ to the front of $$$a$$$.

In order to maintain the number of inversions in $$$a$$$ after each operation, notice that moving the first $$$1$$$ to the end of $$$a$$$ reduces the number of inversions by the number of $$$0$$$s after the first $$$1$$$, or equivalently, the total number of $$$0$$$s in $$$a$$$ minus the number of prefix $$$0$$$s. Similarly, moving the last $$$0$$$ to the beginning of $$$a$$$ reduces the number of inversions by the number of $$$1$$$s before the last $$$0$$$, or equivalently, the total number of $$$1$$$s in $$$a$$$ minus the number of suffix $$$1$$$s.

Maintain a deque containing $$$a$$$, and continuously pop prefix zeroes and suffix ones from the deque. Then, whenever performing an operation, either pop from the beginning or end of the deque and update the number of inversions accordingly by maintaining the number of zeroes and ones in the deque. These operations can also be simulated without a deque by maintaining a left and right pointer, since we never add to the deque after filling it initially.
A bit on the harder side
Ignoring indexes 1 and $$$n$$$, if we remove index $$$i$$$, if we perform an operation on index $$$j$$$, all elements between $$$[i, j]$$$ will also have an operation performed on them.
If we remove index $$$i$$$, and we have to reduce the element at index $$$i+1$$$, $$$i+2$$$, etc, what will we subtract it to?

Removing the elements at index $$$1$$$ and $$$n$$$ in a good array results in the array still being good, since the difference between adjacent elements in the array will never increase. The rest of this editorial assumes the index of the removed element is between $$$2$$$ and $$$n-1$$$. Additionally, the rest of this editorial uses indexing based on the array with the removed element, not the original array.

When removing the element that was originally at the $$$i$$$-th index, we need to repeatedly reduce the element that has been moved to index $$$i$$$ by $$$1$$$ until $$$a_{i-1} + k \geq a_i$$$. We then need to repeat the process for index $$$i+1$$$ and so on until we don't need to perform the operation any more. For any element such that we need to perform an operation on, we will reduce it until it is equal to the previous element $$$+ k$$$, meaning if we have to perform an operation on an element, we have to reduce it to $$$a_{i-1} + k(j-i+1)$$$, where $$$j$$$ is the index of the new element. Therefore, the problem boils down to the largest index $$$j$$$ such that we have to set each each element between indexes $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$ to $$$a_{i-1} + k(j-i+1)$$$.

We can use binary search to find this index. For each check at index $$$b$$$, assume all elements from indexes $$$i$$$ to $$$b$$$ have been set to $$$a_{i-1} + k(j-i+1)$$$ (where $$$j$$$ is the index of the changed element). Then, check if $$$a_{b+1}$$$ (if it exists) is $$$\leq a_b + k$$$. The condition is monotonic: too low of an index and $$$a_{b+1}$$$ won't be good, too high of an index and $$$a_{i-1} + (b - i + 1)k \geq a_b$$$ (where $$$a_b$$$ is the original value at index $$$b$$$, not the modified one), and since $$$a$$$ is initially good, the condition will be trivially satisfied.

Finally, once we know the index required, we need to know the number of operations required: we get the expression $$$(a_i - (a_{i-1} + k)) + (a_{i+1} - (a_{i-1} + 2k)) \ldots + (a_{b} - (a_{i-1} + (b - i + 1)k)$$$, which after rearranging terms can be calculated with prefix sums and arithmetic progression formulas.
A bit on the harder side
Read the solution to problem E first

Let's consider all locations that we have not restricted: we can separate them into 3 categories: the position is forced to be a treasure, the position has no undestroyed that depend on it, and all other positions.

The islands that are considered "non-restricted" form a chain of locations, with each non-restricted chain having a treasure between them. What must be true of the locations in this chain such that no condition is violated?
For every pair of adjacent locations, there must be at least one treasure at one of those locations.
Read the solution to E first to find forbidden indexes. If there is no solution, output $$$0$$$.
There are many solutions to this problem, but here's a particularly elegant one: For all non-forbidden destroyed indexes, there are three possible cases we need to handle:

The element at index $$$i$$$ is required to be a treasure, because some non-destroyed element has only one possible treasure location at index $$$i$$$ because the other position is either restricted or out-of-bounds.

The element at index $$$i$$$ can be anything because no other non-destroyed element cares about whether the element at index $$$i$$$ has a treasure or not (because there exist none or all that exist already have a forced treasure somewhere else)
The element at index $$$i$$$ forms a chain (e.g [$$$-1, 1, -1, 1, -1$$$]) such that we can't freely assign the destroyed indexes to have a treasure or not.

The first two cases are simple to handle: simply multiply by $$$2$$$ for every instance of the second case and ignore the forced cases, but the third case is a bit tricker to handle. The key observation is that when we look at the destroyed elements in the chain, in every pair of adjacent indexes, at least one of the values has to be a treasure. This means that, for a given destroyed index at index $$$i$$$, we can either choose to put a treasure at its position or not put a treasure, but that means we must put a treasure at the next position. This is well known to boil down to the Fibonacci sequence. Our final answer is the product of all cases.
Remember to subtract $$$1$$$ in the case where all elements in the array are $$$-1$$$.
